video_title: Branko Milanovic on What Comes After Globalization | Odd Lots
gist: Economist Branko Milanovic argues neoliberal globalization has expired and been replaced by what he calls 'national market liberalism' — mercantilist, zero-sum external economic policy layered on top of unchanged domestic neoliberalism — with 2016 as the watershed year and Europe, Japan and Korea now converged onto Trump's 2016 China position. He supplies hard distributional data (China's elite income has flipped from two-thirds state to two-thirds private since 1988; Italy's bottom decile has slid from the world's 70th to the 55th percentile) and argues China's growth is now globally inequality-INCREASING, making African and Indian growth the only remaining lever on global inequality. Hosts Weisenthal and Alloway push back on both the security case for reshoring and the claim that Trump's rise is primarily about economic grievance rather than immigration.

themes.theme: National Market Liberalism as the Successor Order

insights.claim: Branko Milanovic frames the post-1974 world as four sequential orders — the New International Economic Order, its failure, the US unipolar moment, and neoliberal globalization — and argues the fourth is now expiring and being replaced by 'national market liberalism,' where activity is reshored and external policy becomes explicitly mercantilist rather than free-trade.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Provides a naming framework for the regime investors are actually allocating into: assume reshoring subsidies and tariff walls are structural policy, not a Trump-cycle anomaly.
insights.quote: where lots of activities would be brought back home and where external economic policies would it be essentially mercantile, logistic and not free trade?

insights.claim: The defining feature of the new order per Milanovic is that liberalism has been amputated only at the international layer — domestic policy under Trump, Macron and others remains substantively neoliberal, so investors should not expect the trade backlash to be accompanied by domestic redistribution.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Implies domestic capital-friendly tax and regulatory policy persists even as cross-border trade and capital rules tighten — a bullish domestic-equity, bearish trade-exposed-margin combination.
insights.quote: But domestically, I really see the administrations like Trump, Macron and others. I see them as essentially continuing with neoliberal policies domestically.

insights.claim: Milanovic characterizes the new international regime as beggar-thy-neighbor and explicitly zero-sum or negative-sum, in contrast to the positive-sum assumption underlying the prior free-trade order.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: A negative-sum policy frame means aggregate global growth and trade volumes are a policy casualty, not just a redistribution of shares — argues for structurally lower global trade multiples.
insights.quote: It's a policy of, you know, beggar thy neighbor to some extent, but certainly zero sum game or even a negative sum game.

insights.claim: Milanovic dates the regime break to 2016 and stresses that the China policies Trump introduced were continued under Biden, only executed more intelligently — meaning the direction of travel is bipartisan and survives US administration changes.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Removes 'the next election reverses this' from the base case for China-exposed supply chains; treat US-China decoupling as a multi-administration constant.
insights.quote: And I think the Trump 2016 for me is the watershed year, because many of the policies that Trump then imposed and regarding China that continued under Biden, they were done in a more maybe intelligent way. But basically they continued.

insights.claim: Faced with the elephant-chart problem — Western middle classes growing at ~1% per capita per annum while the top of Western distributions grew 3%+ under Clinton and China grew fast — the US chose to blame China rather than tax the rich, transfer income and rebuild public education, and Milanovic argues social-democratic capitalism was a live alternative that lost on political expedience rather than economics.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: If the driver is political convenience rather than economic necessity, the policy mix is unstable — a future administration could pivot to domestic redistribution, repricing tax risk on capital.
insights.quote: middle classes of the West have not been doing well. Growth rate of 1% per annum. Per capita.

themes.theme: China's Rich-Poor Duality and the Consumption Puzzle

insights.claim: China is now classified as an upper-middle-income country by the World Bank and is being reclassified as advanced by institutions (Milanovic cites a Chinese academic charged the advanced-country journal submission fee instead of the $50 developing-country rate), yet Chinese citizens overwhelmingly still self-identify as a 'moderately prosperous society.'
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: The self-perception gap matters for policy expectations: a population that doesn't feel rich resists both consumption-led rebalancing and the global responsibilities the West wants China to shoulder.

insights.claim: China's income level remains below France or Italy while its technology level is 'oddly similar' to the United States, producing a country with villages under the $2/day absolute poverty line coexisting with global AI leadership — a duality Milanovic says has no clean historical precedent.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Explains why 'China is weak' and 'China is a peer threat' arguments are both empirically supportable — investors should separate frontier-tech exposure from aggregate-income/consumption exposure when sizing China positions.
insights.quote: And on the other hand, we have them as the leaders in artificial intelligence, so hard to reconcile.

insights.claim: China's consumption-to-GDP ratio sits at roughly 40-45% versus about 70% in the US and 50% in India, and Milanovic argues it should be at least ten percentage points higher — the gap being sustained by wage compression and large retained profits at state-owned enterprises.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Quantifies the rebalancing gap: roughly 10+ points of GDP that Chinese consumer-facing sectors would gain if rebalancing ever actually happened.

insights.claim: Milanovic's contrarian read is that Beijing may not genuinely want to boost consumption, because SOE retained profits are the funding mechanism for directed investment in railroads, AI, space exploration and now aircraft manufacturing, plus political-economic influence in Africa — wage compression is politically tolerable so long as wages still grow 3-5% a year.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: If the low consumption share is a feature funding strategic capex rather than a bug, bets on a Chinese consumer-rebalancing trade are structurally mispriced — the industrial/strategic-tech complex stays favored.
insights.quote: So I think there is a political economy reason behind that in China.

insights.claim: Milanovic argues China's growth has crossed an inflection point: from 1990 until a few years ago it automatically reduced global inequality, but today Chinese growth is mildly inequality-INCREASING at the world level because China is now pulling away from Sudan, Ethiopia and Congo faster than it converges on the US.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Reframes the global development narrative: the single largest engine of falling global inequality has switched sign, so future inequality headlines will get worse even with strong Asian growth.
insights.quote: Chinese growth today is globally inequality increasing. They almost took it like it's an insult. So you're telling us we should not grow?

insights.claim: For the first time in two centuries, the lower parts of Western income distributions are sliding down the GLOBAL distribution — Milanovic's example is Italy's bottom decile, which sat around the 70th world percentile 30 years ago and is now near the 55th.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Quantifies the mechanism behind Western political backlash: absolute incomes barely moved but global rank collapsed, and rank is what voters feel.
insights.quote: In other words, if Italy had qualify for the World Cup, that Italian would not have the money to come to watch Italy.

insights.claim: Milanovic argues global inequality between individuals can only be reduced by high growth in poor countries — making India and especially Africa, where five or six countries hold roughly a billion people and population grows about 2% a year, the decisive variable for the 21st century.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Points frontier-market allocation toward large African economies as the only remaining structural convergence trade; failure there means global inequality rises regardless of Asian performance.
insights.quote: How are we going to have a reduction in global inequality or not if Africa doesn't catch up, we will have another increase in global inequality.

insights.claim: Weisenthal pushes back on the relative-position thesis, arguing that being outranked globally only materially harms Western middle classes for genuinely positional goods — World Cup tickets and Disney vacations — and that the mechanism is far narrower than the political rhetoric implies.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: If the grievance rests on positional goods rather than real consumption, protectionist policy is treating a status problem with an economic instrument — implying persistent policy misfire and continued political volatility.
insights.quote: Yeah, there aren't that many things that are like the World Cup, where the existence of wealthy people elsewhere actually diminishes your relative.

themes.theme: Homoploutia and the Unassailable Folksy Elite

insights.claim: Milanovic coins 'homoploutia' for the empirically new phenomenon whereby a rising share of the US top 10% (roughly 30 million people) are simultaneously in the top decile of both capital income and labor income — unlike 19th-century capitalists such as JP Morgan who drew income essentially from capital alone.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Explains why wealth-tax and capital-gains proposals face broader political resistance than in prior eras: the constituency defending capital income now also earns top labor income and votes accordingly.

insights.claim: Milanovic argues this class fuses meritocratic self-justification, defence of private property and a hard-work ethos into a combination he believes is historically new in capitalism, drawing on Daniel Markovits's work on meritocracy and contrasting it with James Burnham's managerial-class prediction.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: A self-justifying elite is a durable political constituency — expect continued resistance to redistribution and continued fiscal reliance on tariffs and other indirect levies instead.
insights.quote: And that means that the meritocracy, protection of private property, large capitalism and hard working ethos is combined. And I would venture to say this is a new combination in historical capital.

insights.claim: The dual income stream makes this elite structurally shock-proof in Milanovic's telling: if the stock market falls they still have high labor income, so ordinary economic downturns cannot displace them the way they displaced earlier rentier classes.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Predicts that even a severe equity drawdown does not mean-revert US top-decile consumption or political power — a reason luxury and high-end services demand may prove more drawdown-resistant than historical analogues suggest.
insights.quote: because you cannot get rid of them because they have a higher capital income. Since stock market goes down, they would actually have labour income.

insights.claim: Milanovic labels the American version 'folksy elites' — an elite that deliberately performs non-elite status, which Weisenthal concedes he does himself by describing the University of Texas as 'just a state school' while acknowledging it is one of the wealthiest and best schools in the country.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: Signals why elite-status grievance is hard to read from public rhetoric — self-descriptions systematically understate power, muddying sentiment reads on political-economy risk.
insights.quote: oh, I went to a public university at the University of Texas. It's just a state school, which happens to be one of the best schools of the nation and incredibly wealthy.

themes.theme: China's Elite Recomposition and Soft-Power Ceiling

insights.claim: Milanovic's data on the top 5% of China's urban population shows a complete reversal: in 1988 roughly two-thirds of elite income came from state-owned enterprises, government jobs and Communist Party positions, while by 2018 — with data now through 2023 — two-thirds comes from private-sector and professional jobs and only one-third from the state.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Hard evidence that China's wealth base is now predominantly private despite state-capitalist framing — a structural fact often missed by investors modelling China as state-dominated.
insights.quote: And now we have a data for 2023 is the reverse. Two thirds of total income from the elite in the elite for the elite comes from private sector jobs, professional jobs in private companies and one third from state owned enterprises, Communist party and government.

insights.claim: Benchmarking against Bob Allen's data on England's capitalist class between 1688 and 1900, Milanovic finds China compressed the same extensive and intensive growth of a capitalist class into 40 years versus Britain's 150 — a rate of social transformation with no historical equivalent at that population scale.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Supports the view that China is genuinely sui generis rather than a Japan or Soviet analogue — historical-analogy-based forecasts for Chinese growth deceleration are weakly grounded.
insights.quote: and that in China, it took 40 years for that and the UK took 150. So the change in China is just at the level that we have not historically seen.

insights.claim: Milanovic reads Xi Jinping as explicitly reversing Jiang Zemin's 'three represents' doctrine by purging wealthy individuals from Communist Party decision-making bodies — the deal being you may get rich but you may not govern, echoing China's historical treatment of merchants.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Frames Chinese regulatory crackdowns on tycoons as a durable constitutional principle rather than episodic campaigns — political risk for Chinese founder-led equities is structural, not cyclical.
insights.quote: he came and he actually explicitly said that he doesn't want rich people to enter the decision making bodies of the Communist Party.

insights.claim: Milanovic relays a story he flags as possibly apocryphal that Jack Ma was informed his IPO was cancelled by a mid-level Ministry of Finance official rather than the Minister — a deliberate signal of the state's assessment of a billionaire's rank.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Illustrates that in China the channel of communication is itself the policy signal — a useful read on how Beijing telegraphs intent toward private-sector champions.
insights.quote: That was the message you don't read with the Minister of Finance. You treat with the mid-level official. That's your level.

insights.claim: Milanovic argues China is culturally isolationist — it stayed out of the Non-Aligned Movement, kept a deliberately low profile through the 1990s neoliberal hegemony, and its intellectual output is overwhelmingly about China itself.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Suggests China will not build an ideological bloc the way the US did — geopolitical competition stays transactional and economic rather than a mirror-image Cold War of ideas.

insights.claim: Milanovic cites his own Chinese publisher saying Chinese readers will not buy books that are not about China, and contrasts this with Richard Pipes being feted in the Soviet Union in 1989 for having shaped how Russians saw their own history — concluding China's soft power will stay capped until it produces scholars who write about other countries.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: A structural constraint on Chinese influence that is not fixable with money — relevant to anyone pricing the durability of Chinese alliances or renminbi internationalization.
insights.quote: Chinese audience, they don't want to read anything, which is not about China.

insights.claim: Milanovic notes that as recently as ~15 years ago, Nobel Prize-winning economists were writing that China would never develop technologically, and that anyone claiming to have foreseen China's actual trajectory can be checked against the published record.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: A calibration warning: consensus expert forecasts on Chinese technological capability have already been catastrophically wrong once within the current cycle.
insights.quote: and they got Nobel Prize, you know, prizes for writing that China would never technologically developed like 15 years ago

insights.claim: Milanovic is explicitly pessimistic on Europe because it has simultaneously severed the two inputs it needs: it cut off cheap Russian energy that fuelled 40-50 years of growth in favour of more expensive American supply, and it faces population decline while rejecting the immigration that is the only remedy — with Spain under Sánchez the sole outlier.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: A structurally bearish case on European competitiveness and growth — supports persistent European energy-cost disadvantage and demographic drag as a multi-decade rather than cyclical trade.
insights.quote: And so they need people, but they don't want people. They need cheap energy. But they decided to cut off the energy. And then China's shock comes especially to Germany.

insights.claim: Milanovic and Weisenthal agree the entire Western bloc — Europe plus Japan and Korea — has effectively converged onto Trump's 2016 position on China, with Germany's electric-vehicle exposure the sharpest driver of European alignment.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Means Chinese EV and industrial exporters face a coordinated multi-jurisdiction tariff and quota regime, not just a US one — widen the geography of trade-barrier risk in any China auto/industrial model.

insights.claim: Milanovic suspects European sympathy with Trump is substantially feigned — a survival posture he likens to being caged with a tiger and flattering it until it leaves — implying European alignment on China could partially unwind once US leadership changes.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Distinguishes structural European interest (EVs, industrial competitiveness) from tactical accommodation — the former persists, the latter is reversible, so watch which policies Europe keeps after a US transition.
insights.quote: I think actually many people treat Trump like a tiger in a cage. You are with the tiger there and you just want to survive until the tiger is gone, you know?

themes.theme: Security Logic and the Spread of Trade Nationalism

insights.claim: Milanovic sides with Hobson, Lenin, Rosa Luxemburg and Schumpeter over Montesquieu on the trade-and-peace question, arguing large firms competing for foreign markets and control of foreign labor force states into military roles — so openness structurally generates conflict rather than preventing it.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: If openness and conflict are complements rather than substitutes, defense spending and geopolitical risk premia are structurally linked to globalization intensity, not inversely.
insights.quote: well, I agree with Hobson, Lenin and Roger Luxemburg. Openness is war.

insights.claim: Milanovic's sharpest concession is epistemic: if the security-driven view of trade is correct now, then the frictionless world people believed in during the 1990s was never real and the neoliberal ideology underpinning it was a fantasy ideology — not a working model that later broke.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Implies any model calibrated on 1990-2015 trade and cross-border capital behavior is calibrated on an anomaly, not a baseline — a case for structurally rebasing long-horizon assumptions.
insights.quote: that simply means that the world that we believed in 1990 was not the real world. That was a fantasy world.

insights.claim: Weisenthal makes the dual-use argument that losing commercial manufacturing muscle means losing military manufacturing muscle, invoking Alexander Hamilton's claim that a nation without productive capacity lacks sovereignty — the strongest available case for accepting higher consumer prices.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: Frames the political floor under reshoring subsidies: the security rationale is price-insensitive, so industrial-policy spending is unlikely to be repealed on cost grounds.
insights.quote: if you can't build a car, you can't build like you can't build a tank, ultimately right to dual use technologies. You lose that manufacturing muscle

insights.claim: Milanovic concedes the national-security case specifically for great powers — a big power without industrial capacity simply cannot produce helicopters or drones — while insisting the concern should apply to dependence on all countries, since today's ally may not be tomorrow's.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Predicts reshoring pressure extends beyond China to allied supply chains too — friendshoring is an unstable intermediate state, and defense-adjacent domestic capacity keeps attracting policy support.
insights.quote: because then you big powers need helicopters, and they cannot produce helicopters because they don't have any industrial capacity. Yes, they are not going to have helicopters.

insights.claim: Milanovic observes that economists have unconsciously absorbed mercantilist framing, recounting a famous economist on a panel pivoting from general principles to 'for us, the United States, it is bad' — evidence that the intellectual defence of free trade has eroded inside the profession itself.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: The absence of elite intellectual pushback removes a historical brake on protectionism — expect fewer credible institutional voices arguing against tariff escalation.
insights.quote: But you as a general economist, you have to think about whether it is good for the world or not.

insights.claim: Weisenthal argues China anxiety that began in the US in 2016 and spread to Europe will next spread to developing countries with their own industrial ambitions, citing Malaysia limiting low-end Chinese EV imports and Brazil's Embraer facing competition from Comac.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: Flags emerging-market trade barriers as the next leg of China export friction — a risk to Chinese export volumes that is currently underpriced relative to US and EU tariff risk.

insights.claim: Milanovic cites a Foreign Affairs piece by Subramanian and a co-author arguing that because China leads in high-end AND mid- and low-end manufacturing simultaneously, countries that would normally climb into middle-level manufacturing get squeezed out of the development ladder entirely.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: If the standard export-manufacturing development path is blocked, emerging-market growth convergence stories (and the EM equity case built on them) need a different mechanism.
insights.quote: if China is better in high end manufacturing and middle and low level manufacturing than countries that would normally go into middle level manufacturing, actually would be also squeezed out

insights.claim: Milanovic rejects the efficiency-based complaint about China outright — if China is genuinely best at producing X, Y and Z, it should produce them — locating his only legitimate objection in national security rather than in competitiveness or fairness arguments.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Sharpens which protectionist arguments have intellectual staying power: security-framed barriers are defensible and durable, efficiency-framed ones are not and may prove more negotiable.
insights.quote: If China is efficient to good in producing x, y, and z, let them be producing x, y, and z. Why do we complain about this?

themes.theme: Politics of the Backlash: Grievance, Taxes, and What Actually Drove It

insights.claim: Milanovic advocates a wealth tax he calls a 'pedagogical tax' whose purpose is expressive rather than fiscal — to establish that extraordinary wealth does not confer the right to rule — and he explicitly declines to pick a rate between 2% and 20%.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Signals how wealth-tax advocacy is shifting from revenue arguments to political-power arguments, which is harder to rebut on efficiency grounds and therefore more politically durable.
insights.quote: It is better logical, because you have to tell people that with extraordinary wealth you are not going to rule us. And I don't care how many billions you have. You're not going to rule us.

insights.claim: Pressed by Weisenthal on grouping Trump with Xi and Putin as leaders restraining money elites, Milanovic concedes Trump is not actually fighting elites — he is part of the elite, has brought business leaders into government, and taxes capital less than labor — and clarifies his claim was only about the resentment of the 77 million who voted for him.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Separates the demand side (anti-elite electorate) from the supply side (orthodox pro-capital policy) — investors should price the rhetoric and the tax policy independently.
insights.quote: Actually, he is not only part of the elite. He has, as you said, brought them all in.

insights.claim: Weisenthal challenges the economic-grievance explanation for Trump's success, arguing Build the Wall in 2016 and border policy in 2024 were central drivers — making immigration and perceived cultural change, not capitalist inequity, the primary mechanism.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: If the political driver is immigration rather than inequality, then redistributive policy will not defuse the backlash and labor-supply restriction is the more likely persistent policy — a structural wage and inflation input.
insights.quote: a big part of Trump's success specifically clearly has to do with immigration, which is a different story and Perceived cultural change rather than inequities of capitalism or whatever.

insights.claim: Alloway highlights the asymmetry that people upset about stalled wealth accumulation are being offered exclusively outward-facing remedies such as tariffs, with no corresponding domestic policy response — the defining tell of the national market liberalism regime.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: Predicts continued policy escalation abroad because the domestic grievance is never actually addressed — a self-reinforcing loop that keeps trade-barrier risk rising.
insights.quote: And I think it's interesting and telling that the policy solutions to that are all very much focused outward things like tariffs like that rather than anything focused domestically.

insights.claim: Milanovic's 1989 exchange with Jeff Sachs and David Lipton — where he described introducing market mechanisms as an attempt to save socialism and Sachs replied he was trying to bury it — illustrates his framework that stable systems survive by absorbing doses of their opposite, the way Keynesian intervention saved capitalism after the Depression.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for the current transition: the durable outcome is likely a hybrid regime absorbing elements of the system it is reacting against, not a clean victory for either mercantilism or free trade.
insights.quote: I'm trying to bury socialism.

insights.claim: Milanovic's optimistic path out of great-power conflict requires ceasefires in Ukraine-Russia and the Middle East, followed by a renegotiated new Bretton Woods giving China and India substantially greater institutional influence and Europe substantially less, since current institutional weights still reflect 1945 colonial-era Europe.
insights.speaker: Branko Milanovic
insights.so_what: Identifies the concrete precondition and the concrete concession — European loss of IMF/World Bank weight — that any credible de-escalation scenario would require; watch institutional quota reform as the tell.
insights.quote: having, as people have said, a new Bretton Woods and having a solution where actually China would have greater influence. And not only China, India as well. Uh, Europe, definitely much less
